body_markdown:
TikTok has become a major source of entertainment and information for teenagers, but its influence may extend beyond videos and trends. A recent study suggests that the platform can also affect how adolescents think about food, what they crave, and their willingness to try new foods.


The study, published in the *Journal of Nutrition Education and Behavior* in August 2026, explored how teenagers experience food-related content on TikTok. Researchers found that videos featuring recipes, restaurant reviews, food trends, influencers, diet routines and advertisements can capture teenagers’ attention and sometimes make them feel hungry or interested in eating particular foods.


The findings highlight an important question for parents and caregivers: How much influence should social media have over the way young people think about food and nutrition?


## Why Food Videos Can Be So Powerful


TikTok is designed around short, highly engaging videos. Food content can be especially effective because it relies heavily on visual appeal. Close-up images of meals, satisfying cooking demonstrations and enthusiastic reactions can make food appear more desirable.


According to the study, teenagers reported that seeing certain foods on TikTok could increase their desire to eat or try them. Comments from other users, recommendations from influencers and attractive presentations could all contribute to this effect.


The research involved four focus groups with 25 teenagers aged 15 and 16 at a Midwestern high school. Participants described encountering many different forms of food-related content while using TikTok.


These included cooking recipes, viral food challenges, restaurant recommendations, influencer promotions, advertisements and videos showing what creators eat during a typical day.


For teenagers, these videos can feel less like traditional advertising and more like personal recommendations. That distinction may make some content particularly persuasive.


## Influencers Can Affect Eating Habits


One of the study’s notable findings was the role influencers may play in teenagers’ attitudes toward food and dieting.


Some participants said they paid attention to what influencers ate, particularly when those influencers appeared fit or had a body type the viewer admired. This could encourage teenagers to imitate the person’s eating habits in the hope of achieving a similar appearance.


However, appearance-based expectations can be misleading. People have different genetics, lifestyles, nutritional needs and body types. Eating exactly what another person eats does not guarantee the same physical results.


This is especially important when social media content promotes restrictive diets or promises dramatic changes in a short period. A teenager may see a claim suggesting that a particular diet will produce a certain body shape quickly, without knowing whether the information is scientifically supported or appropriate for them.


Social media also tends to show a highly selective version of reality. Influencers may share meals, workouts and lifestyle routines without showing the full context behind them.


## Teenagers Are Not Always Easily Persuaded


The study did not suggest that teenagers automatically believe everything they see on TikTok. In fact, some participants expressed skepticism toward sponsored content.


Teenagers recognized that influencers may be paid to promote products and could therefore have financial reasons for making certain recommendations. This skepticism is encouraging because recognizing advertising and commercial motives is an important part of becoming a critical social media user.


Still, advertisements can be difficult to distinguish from ordinary entertainment. Influencer marketing often blends products into personal stories, reviews or lifestyle content. A viewer may therefore remember a food product as a recommendation from a trusted creator rather than as an advertisement.


Learning to identify sponsored content can help young people evaluate these messages more carefully.


## The Problem of Food Availability


Another issue identified by the teenagers was frustration when they saw foods online that were unavailable locally.


TikTok can expose users to restaurants, snacks and dishes from around the world within seconds. While that can encourage curiosity about different cultures and cuisines, it can also create immediate cravings for something that a teenager cannot easily obtain.


The gap between seeing a food and being able to access it may make the desire feel stronger. Social media can create a sense of urgency around trends, particularly when users see other people trying something at the same time.


This illustrates how TikTok can influence not only what teenagers want to eat but also how quickly they feel they should have it.


## Parents Can Help Build Healthy Media Habits


The research also points to a positive role for parents. Teenagers in the study described situations in which parents helped them question or reconsider what they saw online.


Parents do not necessarily need to monitor every video a teenager watches. Instead, open conversations can help young people develop the skills needed to evaluate food-related claims themselves.


For example, parents can ask questions such as:


- Who created this video?
- Is the creator being paid to promote something?
- Does the person have appropriate nutrition credentials?
- Is the claim supported by reliable evidence?
- Could this advice be unsuitable for someone with different nutritional needs?
- Is the video showing a realistic lifestyle or only a carefully selected moment?


Family meals and shared activities may also provide an opportunity to reduce the amount of time teenagers spend consuming algorithm-driven food content. More importantly, they can create space for conversations about nutrition, body image and social media.


## More Research Is Needed


Although the study provides useful insights, it does not prove that watching TikTok food videos directly causes teenagers to change their diets.


The researchers used focus groups, meaning the findings were based on what participants reported about their experiences and perceptions. More research is needed to determine whether exposure to particular types of TikTok content consistently leads to measurable changes in food purchases, eating patterns or nutritional intake.


Researchers also suggested that the immediate and highly engaging nature of the platform may influence attention and reward-related processes. However, these possibilities require further investigation before firm conclusions can be drawn.


## A Balanced Approach to Social Media and Food


TikTok is not inherently harmful or beneficial when it comes to food. The platform can introduce teenagers to recipes, cooking techniques, restaurants and cuisines they might otherwise never encounter. It can also inspire young people to become more interested in preparing food.


The concern arises when entertaining content becomes a substitute for reliable nutrition information or when unrealistic diets and body expectations begin influencing eating behavior.


Helping teenagers become critical consumers of social media may therefore be more practical than simply telling them to avoid food-related content. Understanding advertising, questioning dramatic health claims and recognizing that bodies respond differently to diets can help young people make more informed decisions.


Ultimately, the new research suggests that TikTok may have a meaningful influence on teenagers’ food-related thoughts and cravings. Parents, educators and healthcare professionals can play an important role by helping adolescents understand that social media is designed to capture attention, and that not every appealing food video represents reliable health or nutrition advice.


### Source


*Journal of Nutrition Education and Behavior* on August 19, 2026.


### Medical Disclaimer


This article is provided for general educational and informational purposes only. It is not intended to provide medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Individual nutritional needs can vary considerably, particularly among children and teenagers. Parents or caregivers who have concerns about a young person’s eating habits, nutrition, weight, body image or health should consult an appropriately qualified healthcare professional. Social media content should not be used as a substitute for personalized medical or nutritional guidance.
